title: Quantum PCP conjecture
formal: Do there exist integers \(k,d\ge 1\) and a rational constant \(\varepsilon \in (0,1)\) such that the following promise problem is QMA-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions? Input is a list of \(m\le (n+1)^{d} k\)-local Hermitian terms \(H_{i}\) on \(n\ge 1\) qubits and rational \(a<b\) in \([0,1]\), with \(0\preceq H_{i}\preceq I\) and \(b- a\ge \varepsilon\). For \(H=(1/m)\sum_{i} H_{i}\), distinguish \(\lambda _{\mathrm{min}}(H)\le a\) from \(\lambda _{\mathrm{min}}(H)\ge b\).
why: This asks whether approximating a quantum system’s energy captures the full difficulty of quantum witness verification. It connects complexity, quantum codes, and local testing.

progress.text: The survey develops the Hamiltonian conjecture and obstacles to quantum PCP constructions.

Bafna–Vyas explicitly describe the general conjecture as open. Their classical private PCP uses $O(\sqrt n)$ queries; stronger parameters depend on a product-expansion conjecture. This does not prove Quantum PCP.

context_blocks.text: The classical PCP theorem replaces full verification by inspecting a small part of a proof with a constant gap. Entanglement and local indistinguishability obstruct a direct quantum analogue.

Normalization makes the target meaningful. Multiplying a Hamiltonian by a large number could enlarge its energy gap, but would also violate the bound on individual terms. The conjecture asks for a constant gap in average local energy while every constraint retains bounded strength.

A useful way to read the two cases is that one input admits a low-energy global state, while in the other every state has appreciably higher average energy. The challenge is to preserve computational hardness at that coarse resolution. Checking a few local terms can detect a constant average discrepancy, but constructing a reduction with that discrepancy is the unresolved step.

answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
definitions: Here \(1\le m\); each term is specified by at most k distinct qubit indices and the complete matrix on those qubits, with rational real and imaginary parts encoded by signed binary numerators and positive denominators. It is tensored with identity on the other qubits. n is written in unary, thresholds in binary rational notation; N counts every supplied bit. \(\lambda _{\mathrm{min}}\) is the smallest eigenvalue. \(M\preceq N\) means that \(N- M\) is positive semidefinite, equivalently \(z*(N- M)z\ge 0\) for every complex vector z. Inputs violating the matrix promises or with \(a<\lambda _{\mathrm{min}}(H)<b\) are outside the promise. QMA consists of disjoint pairs \((Y,N_{0})\) of sets of binary strings with a polynomial-time uniform quantum verifier: on x it uses polynomially many qubits and gates over {H,T,CNOT}, an arbitrary polynomial-qubit witness, and auxiliary qubits initialized to |\(0\rangle\). \(H=2^{- 1/2}((1,1),(1,- 1))\) is the Hadamard matrix, \(T=diag(1,\exp (i\pi /4))\), and CNOT flips its target when its control is 1. A designated final qubit is measured. For \(x\in Y\) some witness gives acceptance probability \(\ge 2/3\); for \(x\in N_{0}\) every witness gives probability \(\le 1/3\). A deterministic machine produces the verifier circuit from x in polynomial time. QMA-hard means that for every such pair there is a deterministic polynomial-time map sending Y into the low-energy case and \(N_{0}\) into the high-energy case, always producing legal instances on promised inputs. Constants \(k,d,\varepsilon\) are shared by the target problem; reduction polynomials may depend on the source promise problem.

importance.reason: A defining quantum-complexity conjecture connecting robust verification, approximation hardness, and the structure of many-body Hamiltonians.

sentences: The quantum PCP conjecture asks whether even a coarse estimate of a quantum system's lowest energy can capture the difficulty of verifying quantum proofs.
The system is specified by local interactions, each involving only a bounded number of qubits.
The target is hardness for distinguishing two possible ground energies separated by a constant after normalizing the total interaction strength.
Normalization prevents a small gap from becoming a constant merely by multiplying the Hamiltonian by a large number.
The problem connects robust quantum verification with entanglement, quantum codes, and the limits of approximation algorithms.
